title: Well spoken
hook: speech that is well spoken, pleasant, true and in line with the teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mara's generals, an army of craving, sloth, fear and doubt. Your line: better to fight than yield. Today closes a week, and it's about the mouth.

Please pass the salt. Running late. Sounds good. A day's talk is mostly words that vanish the moment they're said. A few stay. A sentence someone said to you as a kid can still be sitting there decades later, for good or for ill. The early Buddhist texts give speech close attention. A short discourse in the Sutta Nipata's third chapter sets out what makes speech good. It has four marks, and a poet stands up at the end.
screen: `WORDS THAT VANISH.` → `A FEW STAY FOR YEARS.` → `SUTTA NIPATA 3.3.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells the monks that speech with four marks is well spoken, blameless, not faulted by the wise. The monk says only what is well spoken, not what is badly spoken. Only what is in line with the teaching, not what goes against it. Only what is pleasant, not unpleasant. Only what is true, not false. Every sentence has to pass all four. Then something lovely happens. Vangisa, the poet monk you met three days ago asking after his teacher, stands up and says: something has come to me. And he puts the teaching into verse on the spot. Speak only words that don't torment yourself and don't harm others. Speak pleasant words, words people are glad to hear, without bringing in anything bad. Truth, he says, is the deathless word; on truth the good stand firm. Notice what this is not. It isn't flattery: pleasant is joined to true. And it isn't blunt honesty with no care for the listener: true is joined to pleasant. The two hold each other in check. The week in one breath: a mind unshaken, the old way of the brahmins, the boatman who takes others across, Vangisa's question, the young wanderer's promise kept, and Mara's generals. Today the poet comes back, still finding the right words.
screen: `FOUR MARKS OF GOOD SPEECH.` · `WELL SAID, THE TEACHING, PLEASANT, TRUE.` · `VANGISA PUTS IT IN VERSE.` · `TRUTH IS THE DEATHLESS WORD.` · then, large: `WELL SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you'll need to say today, at work, at home, on the phone. Run it gently through Vangisa's test: is it true, will it harm the one who hears it or you, and can it be said in a way they'd be glad to hear without bending the truth? Find the words, then let them go and rest with the breath.
Well spoken. In the Sutta Nipata, speech that is well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true, all four at once.
Your line: true and kind. Each one keeps the other honest. One more week, done.

howItsDone: Right speech is the third factor of the noble eightfold path, and many Buddhists, lay and ordained, keep a precept against false speech; teachers often give the four marks of well-spoken words as a test before speaking.

pairs: the poet monk who put it in verse
joined to true, so not flattery
joined to pleasant, so not cruelty

myth: in Sn 3.3, speech only has to be true to count as well spoken
it has four marks: well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true.
the poet Vangisa turns the teaching into verse right there
he stands up, says something has come to him, and praises it in verse.
Vangisa calls truth the deathless word
in his verses, truth is the deathless word, and the good stand firm on it.

fork.setup: you're Vangisa. the Buddha has just finished teaching four marks of good speech, and a verse is rising in you. what do you do?
options: keep quiet; it isn't your place.
stand, say something has come to you, and speak it in verse.
write it down later for yourself.
fork.reveal: he stands, tells the Buddha a verse has come to him, and is invited to speak it. the teaching gets its poem on the spot.

original.note: Pali subhasita: well spoken. the Subhasita Sutta is Sn 3.3.

trapdoor: what you thought: good speech just means not lying.
what it means: four marks at once: well said, in line with the teaching, pleasant and true, each keeping the others in check.
what a scholar hears: the Subhasita Sutta (Sn 3.3) is also found in the Samyutta Nikaya, in the section of verses connected with Vangisa (SN 8.5).
guess: speech that is true, pleasant and fitting
speech that is blunt, whatever it costs

chat.says: Isn't being totally honest more important than being nice?
options: The teaching joins them: speech should be true and also pleasant to hear.
Honesty wins; if it's true, how it lands doesn't matter at all.
Only true matters for monks; pleasant speech is for laypeople.
chat.meaning: The four marks join true and pleasant, so good speech isn't flattery and isn't harsh bluntness; each holds the other in check.

Vangisa.meaning: the poet monk who put the teaching into verse

Sutta Nipata.meaning: a small, old collection of mostly verse discourses

Mara.meaning: the tempter, whose generals you met yesterday

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 3.3 (Subhasita Sutta), the four marks and Vangisa's verses

notes: Sn 3.3 paraphrased. Fausbøll's 1881 translation (SBE 10) is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.
